analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from collecting, keeping, or selling people's reproductive and sexual health data without their request.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee: after introduction in May 2023 and referral to the committee, it got no markup, no debate, and no vote before the Congress ended in January 2025, despite 16 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, details like a visit to a clinic or a period-tracker app entry became data that companies can collect and sell, because the health-privacy law HIPAA does not cover most apps and data brokers. This bill would forbid any company covered by FTC jurisdiction from collecting, keeping, using, or sharing personal reproductive or sexual health information except when strictly needed to deliver the service a person actually asked for. It would also give people the right to see, correct, and delete that data, require public privacy policies, ban companies from punishing people who exercise these rights, and let the FTC and individuals sue violators. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use period trackers, fertility apps, telehealth, pharmacies, or search engines — essentially anyone whose reproductive or sexual health data is currently gathered and sold by companies outside HIPAA's reach, in a legal environment where such records can be sought in state-level abortion enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of health apps and anyone with reproductive data online

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits companies from collecting, retaining, using, or disclosing personal reproductive or sexual health information unless it is strictly necessary to provide a service the person requested, covering location data that might indicate a visit to obtain reproductive care.

Gives individuals enforceable rights to access their data (including which third parties it was sold to or collected from), correct inaccuracies, and demand deletion, with companies required to respond within 15 days and forbidden to charge fees.

Lets individuals sue violators for $100 to $1,000 per violation per day or actual damages, plus attorney's fees, treats a violation as a concrete injury for standing, and voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under the Act — meaning people can sue in court rather than being forced into private arbitration.
Enforces the rules through the Federal Trade Commission as an unfair or deceptive practice, and preserves stronger state privacy laws rather than overriding them.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that currently profit from collecting and selling reproductive and sexual health data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and health and period-tracking app makers — plus compliance costs that could be passed to consumers in small ways.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and health app makers

drawbacks.text: The private right to sue for $100–$1,000 per violation per day, plus punitive damages, could generate waves of litigation against companies for technical errors rather than meaningful harm.

The definition of covered information is broad — it includes inferred and algorithmically derived data, and even signs like menstrual symptoms and whether a person is sexually active — which some companies would argue is difficult to implement precisely and could burden small app developers.

Entities covered by HIPAA, such as doctors' offices and insurers acting in that role, are excluded, so the bill would not strengthen privacy in the traditional medical system, only in the largely unregulated app and data-broker market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection addresses a real gap: HIPAA does not reach the apps and brokers where much reproductive data now lives, and the bill closes it with unusually strong enforcement (private lawsuits, no forced arbitration, preserved state laws). The main costs are compliance burdens and litigation risk for companies, some of which would fall on small developers; the strongest objection is the breadth of the covered-data definition, but that breadth is also what stops workarounds where sensitive facts are inferred from ordinary browsing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 2023, and the committee — chaired by a cosponsor of the bill — never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Mazie Hirono introduced the My Body, My Data Act on May 17, 2023, with a group of Senate Democrats including Wyden, Baldwin, Blumenthal, Brown, Cantwell, Duckworth, Gillibrand, Klobuchar, Merkley, Menendez, Shaheen, and Smith as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that was the only action ever taken on it.
Sixteen Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill — none of the 49 Senate Republicans did.
The Commerce Committee, whose chair was herself a cosponsor, never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill received no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and health app makers are better off: they can keep collecting and selling reproductive and sexual health data with no federal restrictions. People who use these services gained nothing, and remain exposed to having their data sold or subpoenaed.

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the Senate.

for.name: 16 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a cosponsor of the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill but never scheduled a markup, hearing vote, or floor recommendation during the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican signed on to the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan base that typically moves a bill through committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; none of the 49 Senate Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where a partisan split could be recorded.

industries.note: These firms buy and sell location and browsing data that can reveal a visit to a clinic or an attempt to obtain reproductive care; the bill would ban collecting or selling such information except to provide a service the user requested. Their revenue model for this data would be shut down, and it is a revenue model that puts ordinary people's most sensitive facts on the market.

industries.industry: Health, period-tracker, and fertility app makers
industries.note: Apps that monetize menstrual, pregnancy, and sexual activity data would have to stop collecting it beyond what the service needs, publish privacy policies, and honor access, correction, and deletion requests. Some could adapt by collecting less data; those built on selling it lose their product.
